mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly uses the universal quantifier for the domain of all integers?
mcqs.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) states that the property holds for every element of the domain. Option B says that for every integer x, adding zero leaves x unchanged, which is true for all integers. Option A and C use the existential quantifier (∃), and option D is false because not every integer squares to 2.

mcqs.question: In a class of students, which statement correctly asserts that at least one student scored above 90 marks?

options.B: There exists a student who scored above 90 marks.
options.D: Every student scored 90 marks or less.

mcqs.answer: There exists a student who scored above 90 marks.
mcqs.explanation: The existential quantifier (∃) expresses that the property holds for at least one element of the domain. Option B captures this meaning. Options A and D describe universal statements, while option C is the negation of the existential claim.

mcqs.question: The English sentence "All prime numbers are odd" is represented by which of the following symbolic statements?
mcqs.explanation: The phrase "All prime numbers" translates to a universal quantifier (∀) over the set of primes ℙ. Hence the correct symbolic form is ∀ p ∈ ℙ, p is odd. Option B mistakenly uses an existential quantifier, and options C and D state incorrect properties about primes.

mcqs.question: What is the correct negation of the statement "∀ x ∈ ℝ, x² ≥ 0"?
mcqs.explanation: Negating a universal statement ∀x P(x) yields an existential statement ∃x ¬P(x). Here P(x) is "x² ≥ 0", so ¬P(x) is "x² < 0". Therefore the negation is "There exists a real number whose square is negative" (option A). The other options either keep the universal quantifier or do not correctly apply negation.

mcqs.question: Which pair correctly contrasts the truth conditions of a universally quantified statement and its existential counterpart?

options.A: ∀x P(x) is true iff there exists at least one x for which P(x) is true; ∃x P(x) is true iff P(x) holds for all x.
options.B: ∀x P(x) is true only when P(x) holds for every element of the domain; ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for at least one element.
options.C: Both ∀x P(x) and ∃x P(x) require P(x) to hold for all elements of the domain.
options.D: ∃x P(x) is false only when P(x) holds for all elements.

mcqs.answer: ∀x P(x) is true only when P(x) holds for every element of the domain; ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for at least one element.
mcqs.explanation: A universal statement (∀) demands the predicate to be true for every element; an existential statement (∃) needs the predicate to be true for at least one element. Option B states this precisely. Options A, C, and D invert or confuse the conditions.

mcqs.question: In the set S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, which statement is logically equivalent to "∃ x ∈ S such that x is a multiple of 3"?

options.A: x = 3 is the only element satisfying the condition.
options.B: There exists at least one element in S that is divisible by 3.
options.C: All elements of S are multiples of 3.
options.D: No element of S is a multiple of 3.

mcqs.answer: There exists at least one element in S that is divisible by 3.
mcqs.explanation: The existential quantifier asserts the existence of at least one element with the property. In S, the number 3 is such an element, making statement B correct. Statement A is too restrictive, C is false, and D contradicts the original existential claim.

mcqs.question: Express the sentence "Some even number is greater than 10" using quantifiers.
mcqs.explanation: The phrase "Some" translates to the existential quantifier (∃). We need an integer n that satisfies both conditions: being even and greater than 10. Option A captures this exactly. Options B and D use universal quantifiers, and option C mentions odd numbers, which is incorrect.

mcqs.question: Negate the statement "∃ y ∈ ℕ such that y is prime and y is even".

options.A: ∀ y ∈ ℕ, y is not prime or y is not even
options.B: ∀ y ∈ ℕ, y is prime and y is even
options.C: ∃ y ∈ ℕ, y is not prime and y is not even
options.D: ∃ y ∈ ℕ, y is prime or y is even

mcqs.answer: ∀ y ∈ ℕ, y is not prime or y is not even
mcqs.explanation: The negation of an existential statement ∃y P(y) is the universal statement ∀y ¬P(y). Here P(y) is "y is prime and y is even"; its negation is "y is not prime or y is not even". Option A correctly reflects this. Options B, C, and D either retain the existential quantifier or apply the wrong logical connector.
